I would keep to the wheat-maize rotation that fits Quzhou County best, because it is the safest and most familiar way for me to make use of my land, water, and labor. At the start of the growing season, my winter wheat is already in the field, so I would manage that crop through spring and early summer, then I would plant summer maize right after wheat harvest. I would not switch heavily into vegetables, cotton, or other cash crops, because at my age I would choose stability, simpler field management, and lower market risk over chasing higher but less certain returns. I would use improved or hybrid seed where it clearly raises yield and reduces risk, but I would still keep management practical and not overly complicated. For wheat, I would use moderate fertilizer, several irrigations if water is available, and a few pesticide sprays only when needed for aphids, rust, or weeds. After harvest, I would quickly prepare the field and sow summer maize, using more nitrogen for stronger growth, with fewer irrigations during the rainy season but close attention to weeds and armyworm or borer pressure. I would use rotary tillage because it is efficient, common, and easier for me than deep ploughing every season. My goal would be steady grain output, manageable labor, and dependable income rather than taking big production risks.
